evaluations.verdict: This is the only concept with real squircle discipline. It is one centred object that fits the 80% maskable circle, the 5 survives at 16px, and the glyph is effectively the icon's tinted-mode silhouette, so Icon Composer's dark, clear and tinted appearances and the template image all come from the same drawing. Its costs are ownership and state: it is the archetypal timer-app icon, and a static 5 inside an open C sits close to the SF Symbols goforward.5 skip control. Next to the clock it also reads like a live value.
evaluations.riff: Merge with runner at the app's true scale. Keep this composition and the 5 as the hero, and perch a small hamster, about a sixth of the ring's diameter, on the leading cap where the app runs it. Echo it in the glyph as a round-eared bump on that cap. That adds ownership and stops the open C reading as a skip-5 arrow.

evaluations.verdict: This is the most ownable art in the round, because the outlined hamster is drawn in the app's own creature style. But it flips the app's hierarchy: in the app the numeral is the hero and the runner is tiny. A hamster inside a ring also flirts with 'hamster wheel', and the ring fills about 90% of the plate, so it crowds the edges and overshoots any maskable crop. The glyph fails outright: at 18pt the leaping body is a splat in a circle, and at 16px @1x on Windows and GNOME it reads as a bug.
evaluations.riff: Draw the glyph head-only: ring's clean 260° C with a round, two-eared hamster head (eye knocked out) sitting in the gap. A body can't survive at 18pt but a head can, and the colour icon can keep the full hamster.

evaluations.verdict: A clean single-object icon that holds up at 16px and shows the randomiser faithfully. On its own, though, it reads as a generic gradient card. The bevelled yellow and navy flecks look like a butter stick and a gem rather than paper confetti, and it drops the rainbow timer that teachers know best. The glyph is crisp but looks like a toaster or a robot face; nothing in it says 'pick a name'.
evaluations.riff: Rebuild it as a vertical reel: three stacked name pills cropped by the window, the middle one solid white and its neighbours half-hidden, with the bevelled flecks removed. The glyph then becomes a framed stack of three pills (middle solid, outer ones at reduced alpha) that reads as 'pick one' instead of a toaster.

evaluations.verdict: It answers the brief literally, timer plus name picker. But the layout pins the card into the top-right corner and the ring against the bottom-left edge, which breaks the macOS keyline and clips badly in a circular maskable crop. The glyph drops the 5 and becomes a key on a tag, or a link symbol. Two unrelated tiny objects at 18pt is one too many.
evaluations.riff: Pull the pair into one centred lockup inside the 80% circle, with the ring overlapping the lower-left third of the card. Keep the 5 inside the glyph's ring so the tiny mark reads as timer plus card rather than a key on a tag.

evaluations.verdict: The die-cut star is a superb silhouette at small sizes, in the warmest palette of the set. But it buries the timer: there is no numeral and half the ring is hidden, so the icon says 'star', everyone's favourites and ratings symbol, not 'rainbow timer'. The glyph dims the whole ring to 50% grey behind a solid star, and in a template image that reads as an inactive ring with a favourite badge.
evaluations.riff: Demote the star. Put the 5 back as the hero, shrink the star to a small rim sticker where the runner rides, and draw the glyph's ring solid rather than 50% grey so the template reads 'timer' first.

evaluations.verdict: Charming as a picture of the board and recognisable at 512px, but it puts four focal points in one squircle (card, star, ring, confetti) and collapses into pink-orange mush at 32 and 16px. The two-tone glyph (grey card blob, star, part-grey C) reads as a reload or cloud-sync symbol and is the least legible of the nine.
evaluations.riff: Retire it as the icon and use it as the About-window or onboarding illustration. If it has to stay, cut it down to the ring plus one sticker, which is dial2.

evaluations.verdict: The celebratory energy is right, but the hero card is small and parked in a corner, the centre of the plate is empty amber with a glow, and the chunky primary-coloured sticks are heavier and cooler than the app's fine paper confetti. At 16px it is a pink rectangle with scratches. The glyph, a box plus sparks, reads as a flash or a 'new' badge rather than a name picker.
evaluations.riff: Fold it into slot. Keep pop's diagonal burst but give the card slot's scale (at least 70% of the plate width), and thin the confetti to three small paper flecks in the app's colours, so the plate isn't mostly empty amber at 16px.

evaluations.verdict: This tells the product story best: four real widgets read instantly as 'Widgets', plural, anchored by the dark traffic light, and it still reads at 32px. But it is four equal focal points jammed into the corners, which fails the keyline and any maskable crop, and tinted mode will flatten them into four grey lumps. The glyph is the dot grid the client wants gone, just with pictures in it, and at 16px @1x on a school PC at 100% scaling the cells close up.
evaluations.riff: Rebalance to one hero plus a supporting cast. Give the ring two-thirds of the plate and shrink the traffic light, card and star into a strip beside it. Cut the glyph down to the ring plus a tiny traffic-light pill, because four equal cells is still the grid the client asked to lose.

evaluations.verdict: A solid variant of ring (big 5, rainbow track, die-cut sticker) that reads very well at 16px. But the magenta heart pulls it toward health or dating-app territory, shoves the 5 off-centre and pushes the ring toward the left edge. The glyph's black C with a heart at four o'clock reads as a 'G', and its 50%-grey spent arc looks like an inactive state in a template image.
evaluations.riff: Move the heart up onto the ring's leading cap at about one o'clock, where the runner rides. The 5 re-centres, the ring comes off the left edge, and in the glyph the heart no longer sits where a G's crossbar would be.

general: All nine now use the app's own visual language (amber plate, rainbow ring, gradient card, die-cut stickers), so recognition is fixed. But the set splits cleanly. The single-hero designs (ring, dial2, slot, sticker) hold up at 16px, and ring is the only one that fits the 80% maskable circle. Every collage (duo, board, pop, gridplus) crowds the plate edges and blurs at favicon size. None of the nine drew macOS 26 dark, clear or tinted appearances: every 'dark desktop' tile is the identical PNG. Several glyphs rely on 50% grey, which reads as an inactive state in a template image, and most glyphs are shrunken icons rather than symbols drawn at SF Symbols weight and checked at @1x for school Windows PCs running at 100% scaling. Two things are missing: the app's most ownable asset at its true scale, a small runner creature riding the ring's leading cap, and a live status item whose ring depletes while a timer runs. Next round should use ring as the chassis, add the runner as the signature, and deliver Icon Composer layers (plate, ring, face, numeral, runner) with dark and tinted variants, a hand-tuned 16px/favicon master without the facets, and an eared-cap glyph tested against the SF Symbols goforward.5 look-alike.

evaluations.verdict: The only concept that survives my whole ladder. At true 1x 16px (the sheet's bars are 2x renders) the white C-ring and heavy 5 stay crisp beside Fluent and Adwaita symbols, the 16px .ico still shows a dark 5 in a rainbow ring, and a circular maskable crop leaves it intact. The risk is meaning, not rendering: a static numeral in a tray reads like an unread count or a 'replay 5' button, and on its own it says 'timer app' more than 'widget toolkit'.
evaluations.riff: Merge with runner: seat the timer's hamster on the arc's leading cap in the colour icon, where teachers see the creature running. Make the tray glyph stateful: ring and 5 when idle, a live depleting arc with minutes left while a timer runs (via Electron's Tray.setImage), so the numeral is true rather than a fake badge. Ship hand-snapped 16/20/24 .ico frames.

evaluations.verdict: The most lovable and ownable colour icon in the set: a hamster in the rainbow ring is unmistakable in an app grid at 48-96px. The traced silhouette fails the tray, though. At true 16px white on the dark taskbar, and even at 22-24px on KDE or at 150% on Windows, the hamster collapses into a splat inside a ring, and the 16px .ico turns it into a brown smudge.
evaluations.riff: Merge with ring: move the hamster off the face onto the ring's leading cap and restore the bold 5. For the tray, use ring's C-ring-and-5 glyph (or a plain round-eared bump at the cap) instead of the traced silhouette, which cannot hold at 16-24px.

evaluations.verdict: The glyph renders crisply, but at true 16px on a Windows taskbar the solid landscape card with a slot rhymes with the battery icon two places over, and the flecks read as sparks. The colour icon reads as a face with eyebrows or a toaster and shrinks to a pink bar on brown at 16px; a circular maskable crop also clips the card corners and the diamond.
evaluations.riff: Replace the landscape card and flecks with a squarer window showing the randomiser's real reel (faded chip, bright chip, faded chip), kept inside the 80% safe circle. The tray silhouette then stops rhyming with the battery, and the icon matches what teachers see.

evaluations.verdict: Two heroes at equal weight leave no single silhouette. At true 16px the glyph is a tiny 'o' beside a tiny card and reads like a link or contact icon. The 16px .ico smears the 5 into a blob that looks like a 9, and a circular maskable crop clips both the card corner and the ring.
evaluations.riff: Fold into ring: use ring's single C-ring-and-5 silhouette for the tray and for the 16-32px .ico frames, and keep the randomiser card only as a second layer in the 48px-and-up art.

evaluations.verdict: The orange die-cut star is the strongest 16px colour element in the set, but it hides the numeral, so the icon reads as 'favourite' or 'rating' before 'timer'. In the tray, the 50%-alpha ring renders as #8f8f8f grey beside crisp white system icons, so it looks disabled and leaves a generic lone star.
evaluations.riff: Put the numeral back on the face and shrink the star to a rim sticker, as dial2 does with its heart. Draw the tray ring at full opacity with a real gap for elapsed time, because half-tone never survives a white 16px tray icon.

evaluations.verdict: At 256px it is literally the board, but it collapses at every size the platforms actually use. At true 16px the glyph is a circular refresh arrow with a speck and a grey smudge, which collides with sync and update-restart indicators, and the 16px .ico is mush. A circular maskable crop clips the card, the confetti and the ring.
evaluations.riff: Retire it as the mark. Keep the composition as a 256px Store/marketing or splash illustration, and ship ring-style single-object art in the 16-48px .ico and hicolor sizes.

evaluations.verdict: One of the crispest tray marks: at true 16px the card plus three strips is asymmetric, sits at the right weight beside Fluent and Adwaita symbols and collides with nothing. The colour icon, though, parks a small card in the lower-left with a lot of empty plate, so at 16px it is a pink speck, and it loses the most to a circular maskable crop.
evaluations.riff: Centre and enlarge the card to about 70% of the plate, with the confetti fanning from behind its top edge inside the 80% safe circle, so the strong tray glyph gets a colour icon with the same presence.

evaluations.verdict: The glyph is legible at true 16px: four distinct shapes survive, if heavy. But a 2x2 of mini widgets in a rounded square is exactly how Windows 11 Start, the GNOME app grid and Android draw a folder, and on the taskbar the four-up white glyph echoes the Start logo and the app-grid symbols the client wants to leave behind. A circular maskable crop clips all four corners, and the 16px .ico is noise apart from the traffic light.
evaluations.riff: Break the four-up grid: make the rainbow timer about 70% of the plate as the hero, with the traffic light and star overlapping its rim as die-cut stickers. That removes the gutters, the folder read and the corner content that gets clipped.

evaluations.verdict: A cleaner cousin of ring whose colour icon holds at 16px: the ring and the pink heart both survive, though the 5 smears, and the heart mostly stays inside a circular mask. The glyph is weaker. The 50% elapsed arc goes dim grey on dark at 16px, leaving a bold C with a blob at four o'clock that reads as a 'G' or a refresh arrow, and the hot magenta heart sits outside the warm dusty-rose family.
evaluations.riff: Merge into ring: adopt ring's full-opacity C-ring and 5 as the glyph. Keep a die-cut sticker on the rim only in the colour icon (a hamster head, or the heart toned to dusty rose), where it adds the sticker vocabulary without costing tray legibility.

general: The contact sheets draw their menu bar, taskbar and GNOME bar at 2x (1400 CSS px captured at 2800), which flatters every glyph. Re-rendered at true 1x 16px, white on #1f1f1f, only the single-silhouette marks stay crisp (ring, pop, gridplus, slot). Anything built on 50% half-tone (sticker, board, dial2) renders as #8f8f8f and looks disabled, and the traced illustration (runner) and multi-object collages (board, duo) collapse. The same split shows under a circular maskable/adaptive crop: the concentric ring designs (ring, runner, dial2) survive, while every corner-anchored composition (gridplus, board, duo, pop, slot) loses content, and those are also the ones whose 16px .ico breaks down. What the whole round is missing is a per-size strategy (Windows .ico and the Linux hicolor theme both allow different art at each size, so 16/20/24 should be hand-snapped simplified frames and 48+ can carry stickers and runners), plus both tray polarities (black for the Windows light taskbar and light KDE panels) and a stateful or live tray glyph. The next round should converge on the ring as the system and add exactly one ownable hook that survives 16px, such as the hamster riding the arc's cap rather than sitting in the centre. It should bring the name picker in through colour rather than a second object, and be judged at true 1x beside Fluent and Adwaita system symbols.

evaluations.verdict: This is the only glyph in the round that comes through 16px intact. The round-capped arc and the single-stroke 5 keep their counters on the light and dark macOS bars, the Windows tray and GNOME. Nobody will mistake it for the clock, wifi or the old dot grid, and it is exactly the colour icon without the colour, so the tray item and the dock icon are clearly one mark. Two small risks remain. The art runs almost to the edge of the 18pt box, so it looks a little heavier than SF Symbols. And a fixed number in a status item can be read as live data, or as a 'skip 5 s' media button.
evaluations.riff: Connect the status item to the running timer: the arc empties in real time and the digit shows the minutes left (1–9, arc only above that), going back to this fixed 5 when idle. The number-looks-like-data risk becomes the reason the tray item is useful.

evaluations.verdict: This is the best randomiser glyph. A chunky card with a big counter plus three short rays reads as one action ('it just popped'), holds up at 16px on dark and light bars, and matches its colour icon closely. The weaknesses: the weight sits bottom-left, so it looks off-centre next to symmetric status icons, and a box with a bar inside drifts towards tray, cast and battery icons.
evaluations.riff: Centre the card in the lower two-thirds and fan the three rays evenly from its top edge. The mark then sits balanced in the bar and reads as one card bursting, not a box with loose dashes.

evaluations.verdict: The shapes are clean and sit well on the pixel grid, the big white counter holds at 1x, and the glyph is a faithful reduction of its colour icon. But a wide, low rounded slab with a bar inside is nearly the macOS battery indicator, which usually sits right beside it. The two confetti specks blur to grey dust at 18px, so the whole thing reads as a toaster, a cassette or a winking face rather than a name picker.
evaluations.riff: Drop the specks, make the card closer to square, and show the faded neighbour chips as stubs above and below the solid chip. A stacked reel can't be mistaken for the battery icon next to it.

evaluations.verdict: The silhouette is bold and crisp at 16px, but it drops the 5 that makes the colour icon a timer. The tray item reads as a heavy 'C' or a refresh arc with a heart, which puts it in health, favourites or dating-app territory. The spent track is drawn at 50% grey, which looks like a disabled item on macOS and almost disappears on the 16px bars.
evaluations.riff: Put the 5 back inside the C, draw the spent track as a clean gap instead of 50% grey, and shrink the heart to a badge on the rim. That turns it into ring plus a sticker, which is the right direction.

evaluations.verdict: This is the most ownable colour icon of the round, but the mono glyph fails at tray size. The diagonal leaping hamster loses everything that identifies it (face, eye, ear colour) and collapses into a lumpy splat. At 16–18px it reads as a flame or a Firefox-style blob inside a refresh arc, and the creature is the one part that doesn't match the colour version.
evaluations.riff: Merge with ring. Put the 5 back on the face and move the hamster to the rim, where the app actually runs it. The glyph becomes ring's arc and 5 with a small head-and-ears knob on the arc's leading end: charming at 36px, and at 18px it just becomes a slightly fatter end cap.

evaluations.verdict: The star is crisp, but it is effectively the whole glyph. The arc is drawn at 50% opacity, which looks like a disabled item on a macOS template image and thins to a faint swoosh on the 16px Windows and GNOME bars. What's left is a generic favourites/starred icon. The colour icon's timer face has no number either, so neither version says 'countdown'.
evaluations.riff: Draw the arc at full opacity, put ring's 5 on the face, and shrink the star to a small die-cut badge on the rim. The timer then carries the silhouette and the sticker is the accent.

evaluations.verdict: At 18px this is an 'o' and a speech bubble on a diagonal. Without its 5 the ring is a meaningless hook, and a solid card with a white bar is the standard chat/message glyph, so the tray reads as chat, link or copy. The diagonal two-object layout also puts the visual centre off-axis among centred system icons, and the 16px favicon shrinks the ring to a speck.
evaluations.riff: Put the 5 back inside the ring and make the ring about 70% of the glyph, with the card reduced to a corner tab tucked behind it. The tray then reads as the timer first, not a chat bubble.

evaluations.verdict: Squint at 16px and it is the 2×2 grid the client asked to get rid of. Each widget gets a cell about 7px wide, so the ring becomes a hook, the traffic light a pill with a hole and the star a blob. It is also the densest, darkest mark in the bar, and it lands right on the launchpad/widgets/category icon convention.
evaluations.riff: Break the grid: make the ring (with its 6) about 70% of the glyph with only the traffic-light pill beside it. Keep the full four-cell layout for the large colour icon only.

evaluations.verdict: This is the weakest tray mark of the round. It is three separate pieces, and the 50% grey card, with its wavy edge where the star and ring clip it, turns into a cloud. At 16–18px the cloud, the star and the crescent-like arc read as a 'clear night' weather icon. The 16px favicon is also a muddle of four elements.
evaluations.riff: Delete the grey card and the confetti, since the card is what turns the glyph into weather, and draw the rest at full opacity: arc and 6 with a small star badge.

general: The 16px test splits the round cleanly. Only ring's arc-plus-digit comes through intact on all three bars and is visibly the same mark as its colour icon; every glyph built on a pictorial element (hamster, star, heart) or on three or more parts collapses into a blob, a favourites star or, in board's case, a night-weather icon. Sticker, board and dial2 use 50% opacity, which looks like a disabled item on macOS and washes out at 16px, so partial opacity should be banned in the glyph. Duo and dial2 dropped the digit, the most legible and most on-brand element; gridplus squints straight back into the grid the client wants gone; and both randomiser glyphs end up as a box with a bar that edges towards the battery and tray icons. Missing from the round: a runner that survives at tray size (as a knob on the arc's leading end, not a full-body silhouette), live states for the tray item (arc emptying, minutes left), a stroke-weight and size spec matched to SF Symbols, Fluent and Adwaita (every glyph here runs almost edge to edge and is heavier than its neighbours), and checks on a light Windows taskbar and at 20/24px tray sizes. The next round should lock ring's arc and digit as the tray glyph, put the daring into the colour icon and motion (runner at the rim, die-cut rim, live countdown), and prove each version beside real system icons at 1x from a hand-tuned 16px master.

evaluations.verdict: This is the most finished and memorable mark in the set. The round-capped rainbow arc on amber holds on every surface down to the 16px favicon, and the 5 has classroom meaning (the five-minute warning, 'give me five'). It is hard to own, though: a numeral inside a multicolour ring is how Google One's logo is built, menu-bar timer apps are full of ring icons, and the glyph is close to SF Symbols' 'gobackward.5' (skip back 5 seconds) minus the arrowhead.
evaluations.riff: Merge with runner. Put a tiny runner nub, drawn like the in-app hamster (ears plus an eye cut-out), on the arc's leading round cap, and draw the spent track as a hairline in the glyph. That gives the mark something no competitor has, and the glyph stops reading as a media skip button.

evaluations.verdict: This has the most brand potential in the set. None of Classroomscreen, Google Classroom, Canva, Notion, M365 or Slack has a character, and the app already has a six-creature cast to build on. As drawn, though, the hamster sprawls like a flying squirrel, looks nothing like the chunky in-app runner, and fills the face instead of running on the ring. The glyph collapses into a blob inside a ring that looks more like Firefox's fox-and-globe than a hamster.
evaluations.riff: Redraw the hamster to match the in-app one and make it small, running on the arc's leading tip, with the numeral back on the face. That is the same merge as ring's riff. In the glyph, reduce it to a head-and-ears silhouette on the arc end instead of a full-body shape.

evaluations.verdict: Regular users will recognise the randomiser, but little here is ownable. The purple-pink-amber window is essentially Instagram's gradient, the blank chip is generic picker UI, and the two floating flecks read as a sticky note and a gem. In the glyph those flecks become angry eyebrows over a grimace, so the menu-bar item looks like a grumpy robot or a toaster.
evaluations.riff: Remove the two symmetric flecks that make the face. Instead, let one off-centre confetti burst come off a tilted card with a sticker border, as pop does. Put a bold initial on the chosen chip, and warm the window toward rose-to-amber to move away from Instagram.

evaluations.verdict: At dock size it reads as 'timer plus name picker', but a mark made of two objects gives people two things to remember and no single shape to build an identity on. From 32px down, the 5-ring looks like a numbered pool ball beside a pink chat bubble. The glyph, an open ring hooked to a slotted tag, reads as a chain link or key fob and says nothing about timers or pickers.
evaluations.riff: Merge the two into one object: make the gradient slot window, with its chosen chip, the ring's face. Keep the faded neighbour chips above and below so the glyph doesn't read as a minus sign in a circle.

evaluations.verdict: The die-cut sticker look is something this brand could genuinely own, but a five-point star is the most generic symbol in edtech: gold stars, favourites, ratings, reward charts. With no numeral, the ring reads as a colour wheel or a loading ring, and the glyph with its grey track looks like a 'refresh favourite' button.
evaluations.riff: Drop the star and make the rainbow timer itself the tilted die-cut sticker, with a thick white border, a slight lift and the 5 on its face. The sticker border then becomes the style used across docs and marketing, instead of carrying a clichéd symbol.

evaluations.verdict: At 128px it is a faithful, charming thumbnail of the board, but it is an illustration, not a mark. It has four elements, no hero and nothing to own, and it shows the category (Classroomscreen also has a timer and name picker) more than this brand. At 16px it turns to confetti-coloured mush, and the glyph (grey cloud, star, open ring) reads as a weather icon or 'refresh favourite'.
evaluations.riff: Delete the card and the star. Keep the 6-ring as the hero and let three flecks of the app's real confetti colours spill out of its empty gap, so the board's energy fits in one shape with a glyph that holds up small.

evaluations.verdict: The most emotional of the randomiser ideas, capturing the moment the class cheers. Its glyph beats slot's because the off-centre card with burst marks doesn't read as a face. But the card is a small element in the lower left, the confetti looks like chunky sticks, the gradient is Instagram's again, and at 16px it is just a pink square on brown.
evaluations.riff: Make the card the hero, tilted like a die-cut sticker and filling about 60% of the tile, with the confetti bursting out of the chosen chip itself. Warm the window gradient so it stops echoing Instagram.

evaluations.verdict: This is the most honest description of the product, keeps continuity with the well-liked 3×3 tile icon, and has the strongest app recognition in the set, plus a legible glyph that suits a launcher. It is also the least ownable: a symmetric 2×2 of coloured tiles is the default image for widget apps, looks like Microsoft's four squares at 16px, and shows Classroomscreen's features as much as this app's. The bento-grid style will date.
evaluations.riff: Break the symmetry: let the rainbow timer take about two-thirds of the tile, with narrow traffic-light and name-picker cells beside it. It then reads as 'the rainbow-timer app' rather than a generic widget grid. Drop the star cell from the glyph so it holds at 16px.

evaluations.verdict: A cleaner, flat poster-style version of the ring that holds up well at 32 and 16px. But the hot-pink heart pulls the meaning toward health, dating or 'likes' rather than classroom time. The glyph drops the numeral, so the menu-bar mark is a C with a heart that looks uncomfortably like a 'G', which is a bad look for a product that sits next to Google Classroom.
evaluations.riff: Drop the heart, or keep it for campaign art only, and carry dial2's flatter poster rendering over to ring. Keep the numeral in the glyph so the icon and the glyph share the same hero.

general: All nine concepts are pictures of the app's widgets on the same amber plate. That gives a strong family look: amber stands out in docks full of blue and green edtech icons, though the low-poly facets disappear below 64px and look dated. Only ring and runner work as marks built on one memorable idea; every concept that combines several objects (duo, board, gridplus, pop) either turns to mush at 16px or ends up with a glyph that means nothing. The rainbow ring appears in six of the nine and is the only element that holds from dock icon to favicon to tray, yet the runner creatures, the most ownable thing the app has, appear once and don't match the app's drawings, and nothing ties back to the Classroom Widgets name. Several concepts also borrow other brands' looks: a numeral in a multicolour ring (Google One), SF Symbols' skip-back-5 icon, Instagram's gradient on the name-picker card, Microsoft's four squares, an orange creature in a ring (Firefox), and a C with a heart that reads as a G. Next round should merge ring and runner: the round-capped rainbow arc as the fixed brand shape, a small runner drawn like the in-app hamster at its leading tip, and the numeral free to change (a favicon that counts down live, numbered campaigns). The 16px glyph should be designed first, and a die-cut sticker border should be tested as the style that runs across web, docs and marketing.

evaluations.verdict: This is the one I'd find in my dock without thinking. It's the rainbow timer my class stares at every lesson, the big 5 is exactly the 'five minutes left, everyone' moment, and it still reads at 16px on a 1x screen and in every menu and tray bar. The honest catch is that it's literal enough to pass for any Pomodoro timer, so from the icon alone I'd guess 'timer app', not a whole classroom toolkit.
evaluations.riff: Keep the silhouette and glyph exactly as they are. Tuck the timer's hamster onto the purple leading cap at 8 o'clock, small, side-on and in the app's dark-outlined cast style (a merge with runner). That adds the warmth and an 'our app' wink at dock size and simply disappears at 16px.

evaluations.verdict: My gut says 'aww': it's the warmest, most daring concept here. But the hamster is huge and leaps diagonally across the face instead of running on the ring, so it reads as a kids' pet game I'd hesitate to put on a secondary-school laptop. At 16px it becomes an orange smudge in a rainbow ring, and in the menu bar the glyph's silhouette is an unreadable blob.
evaluations.riff: Merge into ring: put the bold 5 back on the face and shrink the hamster to a side-on runner sitting on the ring's leading cap, drawn in the app's outlined cast style rather than this softer kawaii version. The glyph drops the silhouette and becomes the C-ring plus 5, with at most a tiny ear bump on the cap.

evaluations.verdict: If you've used the name picker, the purple-pink-amber window is unmistakable. But the chip is blank, so from the icon alone I'd guess a label maker, gift card or toggle switch rather than 'pick a student', and the two flecks read as an eraser and a gem, not confetti. The glyph is crisp but looks like a toaster, or a grumpy face with slanted eyebrows.
evaluations.riff: Put a dark text bar or one bold initial in the white chip so it reads as a name, and let the faded names above and below form a clear vertical reel. In the glyph, drop the two flecks that cause the toaster/face read and use three stacked pills with the middle one solid inside the frame.

evaluations.verdict: This is the closest to the brief. I recognised both the timer and the name picker straight away, and it feels like my actual board: warm and useful. But the card on its own looks like a chat bubble, the two objects share billing so neither owns the icon at 16px, and the glyph (a ring plus a flag) reads as a key and tag.
evaluations.riff: Make the ring and 5 the clear hero at about 70%, with the card peeking out behind it. Give the card its real purple→pink→amber sweep and a dark name bar so it stops reading as a chat bubble. For the glyph, borrow ring's C-ring with the 5 and tuck a small card corner behind it at the upper right.

evaluations.verdict: A gold star is the most 'teacher' symbol there is, and this die-cut star matches our real sticker and stays crisp at 16px. But it covers half the timer and there's no number, so the ring reads as a 'C' or a loading spinner, and I'd guess a class-rewards points app. The grey-ring glyph looks like a generic 'favourites' star.
evaluations.riff: Shrink the star to a rim sticker sitting in the ring's pale spent gap, so the 5 goes back on the face and the star becomes a wink rather than the headline. That makes it essentially ring plus a gold star, which beats dial2's heart for teacher meaning. Draw the glyph's ring in solid black, not grey.

evaluations.verdict: At full size it made me smile, because it's literally my projected board. But it's a collage: busy at dock size, pink-orange mush at 16px, and the glyph (grey card, star and ring) reads as a sync icon next to a cloud. Of the nine, it's the one I'd struggle most to spot in a Windows taskbar.
evaluations.riff: Cut it to two elements, the ring with its number and the star slapped on the rim, and drop the card and confetti. If the collage has to stay for the big icon, make the favicon and glyph the ring and number only.

evaluations.verdict: It's festive and true to the moment the class cheers. But the card is small and pushed into a corner, the confetti reads as three popsicle sticks over a lot of empty amber, and from the icon alone I'd guess a party or event-ticket app. The glyph, a card with burst lines, is clean and does read as 'something just popped'.
evaluations.riff: Centre and enlarge the card, turn it into a vertical reel with a dark name bar in the chosen pill, and swap the three sticks for a halo of small real-confetti flecks in the app's red, yellow, teal and navy. Keep the glyph's burst lines as they are.

evaluations.verdict: From the icon alone I'd guess exactly what this is: a classroom toolkit with a timer, traffic light, name picker and stickers. The traffic light shouts 'classroom', and the whole thing feels organised and trustworthy. But it's the least daring, it looks like an app folder at 16px, and the glyph is still a grid, just a busier one than the dot grid the client wants gone.
evaluations.riff: Break the even 2x2. Let the rainbow timer take about 60% as the hero, run the traffic light horizontally along the bottom the way it actually appears in the app, and make the card and star small satellites, so it reads as one app rather than a folder. Cut the glyph to just the C-ring and the traffic-light pill.

evaluations.verdict: It's bold and poster-clean, and the 5 still reads at dock size. But the pink heart pulls the meaning toward 'likes', health or a favourite timer (I half-read '5 ♥' as five likes), and the app's own heart stickers are blue and teal, not pink. The glyph drops the 5 and becomes a 'C' or 'G' with a heart and a faint grey arc.
evaluations.riff: Swap the heart for the gold star, which is our real sticker and means teacher praise rather than 'like' or health. Shrink it to a wink on the spent track, and keep the 5 in the glyph with no grey arc. It then lands on ring plus a sticker, which is the right place to end up.

general: The rainbow ring is the strongest 'that's our app' cue in the set, and the concepts that keep a readable number on a big, clean ring are the ones a teacher would actually find in a dock, taskbar or browser tab; ring is far ahead there. Collages (board, gridplus, duo) and the randomiser's blank white pill, which reads as a chat bubble, label or toggle but never a name, lose their story below 32px. All nine also sit on the same amber low-poly plate, whose facets vanish at small sizes and whose margin takes pixels from the hero, and none uses the sage/terracotta/dusty-rose brand palette. Glyphs that rely on 50% grey (sticker, board, dial2) look disabled in a menu bar and smear on the 1x screens most school PCs still have; only ring's 5 in a C-ring is instantly 'ours'. Next round: lock ring's silhouette and glyph as the backbone and add one daring, warm wink to it (the runner on the leading cap, a small gold-star sticker in the spent gap, or the randomiser gradient on the face), and judge every candidate at 16px on a 1x display, not on retina contact sheets.

evaluations.verdict: The only concept that passed every check I ran. At a true 16px (1x) the dark 5 holds 10.5:1 on the cream face, the ring and spent gap survive protan/deutan/tritan and greyscale, and the glyph (one opacity level, ~2px strokes, a 1.6–1.8px open counter in the 5) stays crisp on every bar. Its weaknesses are about genre, not legibility: a number inside a ring is close to generic countdown apps, it says nothing about the name picker, and a static 5 in a menu bar can be misread as live status.
evaluations.riff: Make the menu-bar glyph stateful: when idle it shows the C-ring and the 5, and when a timer runs it shows the live minutes with the ring running down. That turns the numeral from a false status into a feature. Also ship hand-tuned 16/24px versions with a spent gap of at least 3px and no bevel.

evaluations.verdict: The most ownable colour icon, but the hamster is smaller than the pixel grid can hold. At 16–18px it collapses into a splat inside a ring, its leg merges into the rainbow (orange fur vs orange segment is 1.26:1), and fur on the cream face is only 2.38:1, so the favicon is an orange smudge. The ring alone carries recognition, and a hamster in a circle also invites a 'hamster wheel' reading.
evaluations.riff: Merge into ring: move a smaller runner back onto the ring at the end of the spent gap, as in the app (a die-cut silhouette from 64px up, a simple notch at 16–32px), and give the face back to a bold numeral.

evaluations.verdict: The glyph is crisp (2.5–3.3px walls and a 3px counter at 18px), but its meaning is not: two flecks over a slotted box reads as a toaster or a grimacing face. In colour, the one signal that means 'name picked', the white chip, is only 1.5–2.6:1 against the pastel window and nearly vanishes in greyscale and deutan views, so at 16px the icon is a pink rectangle on amber.
evaluations.riff: Put a dark name bar or a bold initial on the chip (the app shows black names, 7:1 or better) and deepen the ends of the window, so the chosen row stands out by brightness, not just by hue.

evaluations.verdict: Two widgets at half size each drop below the size where they still read. The 5 is mush at the 24px Windows taskbar size, the ring has no rim and its red, blue and purple segments are about 1.1:1 against the amber, and the chip is 2.3:1 on its pink. In the glyph, the small ring plus the notched card reads as a link or chat icon.
evaluations.riff: Collapse to one shape: set the slot window and chip inside the timer's face so the ring becomes the frame, and keep a single ring stroke in the glyph.

evaluations.verdict: The star only holds up because of its white die-cut border (3.5:1). Its orange fill is 1.49:1 against the amber and turns olive-on-olive for protan/deutan viewers. The glyph draws the whole timer ring at 50% opacity: 3.03:1 on a clean light menu bar, under 3:1 on a tinted translucent one, and the usual 'disabled' look. So the menu-bar mark reads as a star with a loading spinner, and the colour face has no numeral.
evaluations.riff: Make the glyph's ring solid and separate the star with a 1.5px cut-out gap instead of using opacity. Put a numeral back on the colour face so the timer half of the idea survives.

evaluations.verdict: A convincing thumbnail of the board at 512px and the worst performer at small sizes. At 16px the timer, card, star and confetti turn into noise pixels, and the glyph stacks three objects at two opacity levels, so nothing reads at 18px. Only the 6 (10.9:1) comes through the colour-blind and greyscale checks intact.
evaluations.riff: Keep it as the splash screen or marketing illustration and take one element (the ring with its numeral) as the icon. If it stays as the icon, drop the card and confetti and remove all partial opacity from the glyph.

evaluations.verdict: A good emotional idea, and the glyph (a box plus three sparks) is crisp and reads as 'celebrate'. But the confetti is the least colour-blind-safe element in the set: the red strip is 1.08:1 against the amber and disappears for protan/deutan viewers and in greyscale, the navy dots are 1.7:1 in the shaded corner, and the chip is 2.2:1 on its pink, so the 16px favicon is a pink box with two flecks.
evaluations.riff: Pick confetti colours that differ in brightness from the amber, not just in hue: white or cream, lemon and sky-blue die-cut pieces, no red on amber. Use three larger pieces and add a dark name bar to the chip.

evaluations.verdict: The glyph is surprisingly legible (2.4px ring stroke, ~1.7px counters), and the traffic light is encoded correctly: position plus a lit lamp at 8.7:1 against unlit lamps at 1.17:1, so nothing critical depends on hue. But it is still a grid. The 16px colour icon is four 6px blobs with an unreadable 6, and the 2×2 glyph falls in the same generic apps/widgets family as the dot grid the client wants gone.
evaluations.riff: Break the grid: give the ring three-quarters of the tile with the traffic light as a slim vertical pill down the right edge. The glyph then has two elements (ring plus bar) instead of four.

evaluations.verdict: Works at 32px, but the pink heart and the amber plate have identical brightness (1.00:1). Deutan viewers see a grey heart on an olive plate, separated only by a white border about 1px wide at 16px, and the rimless ring's red end (1.04:1) melts into the amber. The glyph drops the numeral and adds a 50%-opacity elapsed arc, so the menu-bar mark reads as a 'G' or a favourite button rather than a countdown.
evaluations.riff: Merge with ring: use ring's C-ring-and-5 glyph with a solid heart sitting in the spent gap. In colour, add the white rim around the ring and darken the heart towards #d42a80 with a thicker border.

general: Only the signals that differ in brightness survive. The dark numerals (10.5–10.9:1 on cream) pass every colour-blind simulation and the true 16px render, while chips, stars, hearts and confetti differ from their surroundings mostly by hue, at 1.0–2.6:1. They hold up only where a white die-cut border outlines them, which makes that border the set's best accessibility feature; pop's red confetti has no border, sits at 1.08:1 on amber and vanishes for red-green colour-blind viewers. Designs with several objects (board, duo, gridplus) fall apart below 32px, and the contact sheets hide this because they were captured at 1.4x pixel density, so their '16px' is really about 22 device pixels. Three glyphs (sticker, board, dial2) use 50% opacity, which gives about 3:1 on a clean light menu bar, less on tinted translucency, and reads as 'disabled', so glyphs should be one solid tone; separately, every amber plate disappears on the app's own amber canvas (1.07:1) and needs a cream outline for in-app and PWA splash use. The next round should build on ring and add exactly one ownable detail that stands out by brightness and survives a true 16px (a runner notch at the end of the spent gap, or a heart in the gap), with hand-tuned 16/24/32px versions and a menu-bar glyph that works as a live countdown.

evaluations.verdict: This is the only drawing in the set that is fully resolved. The arc has one weight and true round caps, the 5 sits optically centred on the face, the top-lit shadows agree, and the glyph redraws the 5 as a monoline at the arc's weight instead of shrinking it, so it holds at 16px and at 18pt. But it is the obvious answer, a number inside a progress ring, and the glyph sits uncomfortably close to a 'skip back 5s' media control or a live countdown badge. It is safe rather than owned.
evaluations.riff: Merge with runner. Seat a small die-cut hamster on the violet leading cap at 9 o'clock, running along the arc the way the creature does in the app. In the glyph, replace that cap with a two-ear hamster head so the mark stops reading as a media control. This keeps ring's geometry and adds runner's character.

evaluations.verdict: This is the only concept with a character the app can own, and its thin, glowing ring running green to violet is the closest copy of the real timer; it is the one direction with a point of view. But the hamster floats splayed in the middle of the face like a flying squirrel and never touches the ring it is meant to push off. The glyph silhouette turns into a lumpy splat by 18pt, so it fails the menu-bar half of the brief.
evaluations.riff: Put the hamster where the app puts it: mid-stride, straddling the ring near the leading cap, as a die-cut sticker in the spot dial2 uses for its heart. Bring back a numeral on the face. Redraw the glyph creature as a bean body with two round ears and a knocked-out eye, at least 8px tall at 18pt.

evaluations.verdict: The gradient window matches the real randomiser, but the chip is blank, so the card reads as a generic toggle or search field. The 'confetti' are bevelled 3D solids (a butter pat and a navy gem), not paper flecks, and two marks over a wide slot make both the icon and the glyph read as a face with a gritted mouth, or a printer. Meanwhile the card crowds the edges of the plate and the top third is empty canvas.
evaluations.riff: Tilt the card about 8 degrees like a sticker and let the white chip overhang the frame to show the moment it lands. Replace the gem and butter pat with three thin, flat flecks fanning from one corner so the face goes away. That brings it close to pop, so merge the two.

evaluations.verdict: Two decent objects sit in opposite corners with nothing tying them together. It reads as two app icons taped side by side, leaves two empty quadrants, and pushes the ring so close to the squircle's corner curve that it looks cropped. The glyph, a C touching a notched tag at one point, reads as a hook, key or plug, and a circular PWA mask would cut into both shapes.
evaluations.riff: Pick one hero. Either let the ring fill the plate at ring's scale with only a sliver of the name card peeking from behind one edge, or drop the card entirely.

evaluations.verdict: This has the best sticker craft in the set: a thick, even die-cut border, a soft shadow and a confident tilt that really looks slapped on. But the gold star is the classroom version of the apple and reads as 'favourites' or 'achievements' in a dock, and without a numeral the timer becomes a generic loading ring. In the glyph, the 50%-grey arc fades on the taskbar and GNOME bar, leaving a lone star.
evaluations.riff: Keep the slapped-on gesture but make the sticker the runner hamster instead of a star, and bring back the numeral. Draw the glyph's arc in solid black, with a gap cut around the sticker instead of the grey.

evaluations.verdict: It is a faithful thumbnail of the projected board, which is exactly why it fails as a mark. Four stacked layers collide everywhere (the star touches the card's edge, the ring clips its corner), the hairline confetti disappears by 32px, and nothing is the focal point. The glyph is the weakest in the set: a grey smudge, a star and a broken ring that blur together at 18pt.
evaluations.riff: Cut it down to two elements, the timer and one sticker, which turns it into dial2. Keep this layout for a marketing illustration or splash screen, not the icon.

evaluations.verdict: This is the freshest take on the randomiser. Flat confetti in the app's real colours fans out of the card's corner with a warm glow behind the burst, and the glyph uses the familiar 'object plus burst lines' pattern, which stays crisp at 18pt. But the card is pushed into the lower-left corner with a blank chip, so at 16px it is just a pink rounded rectangle, more ticket or gift card than name picker, and a circular PWA mask would clip its corners.
evaluations.riff: Scale the card up to about 60% of the plate and tilt it. Trim the burst to the same three flecks the glyph uses. Put a single bold initial in the chip so it reads as a name that has just landed rather than an empty field.

evaluations.verdict: Every object is well drawn, and the glossy traffic light is the best single widget in the round. But this is the generic grid the client already rejected, with widgets dropped in: the heavy navy traffic light pulls the eye, the bento compartments are never actually drawn, and at 16px it is four specks. Worst of all, the glyph is a 2x2 grid again, the exact thing the client asked to replace.
evaluations.riff: Give it a hierarchy. Let the timer take three quarters of the plate and tuck the traffic light, card and star into the leftover L-shape as small tiles. Drop the grid from the glyph and use the ring alone.

evaluations.verdict: This is the best-composed of the timer-plus-sticker ideas: the ring is poster-sized, the main and secondary elements are clear, the sticker overlaps the rim with convincing depth, it holds at 16px, and the C-and-heart glyph is crisp. But a rainbow ring with a pink heart is the shorthand for fitness and health apps (and for 'like'). The numeral is pushed small and up-left so the face loses its centre, and the glyph drops the numeral altogether, which makes the health reading stronger.
evaluations.riff: Swap the heart for the runner hamster as a die-cut sticker in exactly this rim spot, where the app's creature actually runs. Re-centre a heavier numeral at ring's weight. This is the strongest merge available in the round.

general: Round 2 swung from abstract tiles to near-literal copies of the app's widgets. All nine share one amber plate and one rendering style (soft gradients, white sticker borders), so the set is coherent but samey, and most concepts draw widgets rather than make a mark. Only the single-hero discs (ring, runner, dial2) hold up in the menu bar, at 16px and under a circular PWA mask. The collages (board, duo, gridplus) and the corner-placed randomiser cards (slot, pop) blur or clip, and the blank name chip makes the randomiser read as generic UI. The stock stickers (gold star, heart) and the grid are classroom clichés that push the icon toward a rewards, health or utilities app. What's missing is the one character the app can own, the runner creature, drawn with ring's discipline: next round should combine ring's geometry (round-capped rainbow arc, centred numeral, die-cut rim) with a hamster on the rim where the app puts it (dial2's sticker spot), and make that creature a legible 18pt silhouette before polishing anything else.

evaluations.verdict: The only concept where the whole system falls out of one element: the glyph is the icon without colour, the 5 still reads at true 1x 16px, the centred disc survives ChromeOS and Android circle masks and works without its plate on the amber canvas, and the arc gives you a loader and a live favicon, menu-bar and Dock countdown for free. It's the safest idea, though: it says 'timer', not 'toolkit', and a static 5 in a C-ring reads close to a 'skip 5 s' media glyph or a badge count.
evaluations.riff: Merge in runner: put a small hamster on the rim riding the arc's leading cap, as it does in the app, and give that cap two ear bumps in the glyph. Then spec a live state where the menu-bar glyph and favicon show the real minutes and arc while a timer runs.

evaluations.verdict: Richest in 'moves': the app already animates the hamster lapping the ring, and the creature cast plus calm/shocked poses hand you alternate icons, loader, empty, error and time's-up states. But the system breaks at the bottom: the full-body silhouette becomes a house-like blob at 16-18px, and the diagonal diving pose reads as falling out of the timer rather than running on it.
evaluations.riff: Pose the hamster running along the inside of the track, as in the app, with a numeral back on the face. Replace the full-body glyph silhouette with a round head and two ear bumps as the arc's leading cap: it stays legible at 16px and doubles as frame one of the loader.

evaluations.verdict: A good favicon (the pink card holds at true 16px), and the idea carries the round's second-best motion: the reel spins as a loader, then lands with confetti as the success beat. The static frame is inert, though: the card reads as a TV or credit card, the two flecks look like a butter pat and a gem (angry eyebrows in the glyph), and a circular maskable crop shears off the card's sides.
evaluations.riff: Make the static frame imply the spin: square the card up so it's safe in a circle mask, streak the neighbour chips vertically with motion blur above and below the landed chip, and swap the gem and butter flecks for pop's flat strips firing from one corner.

evaluations.verdict: Meets the brief literally (timer plus picker), but the system has no hero: two half-size widgets fight at every size (the 5 is a grey smudge at 16px), and the glyph reads as a chain link or key. A circle mask clips both objects, and any animation splits attention between an arc and a reel.
evaluations.riff: Nest, don't stack: fill the ring's face with the randomiser's purple-pink-amber gradient behind a white chip carrying the 5. One circular object then carries both widgets, survives masks, and keeps ring's glyph.

evaluations.verdict: The die-cut star is beautifully made, and the 'slap' is a great reward micro-interaction, but as the mark it hides the timer, drops the numeral, and brings favourites/bookmark meaning into the browser tab (right beside Chrome's bookmark star) and the menu bar. The glyph's 50% grey ring dissolves at 1x, leaving a lone star.
evaluations.riff: Drop the star. Make the rainbow timer itself the die-cut sticker (thick white border, about 8° tilt, one lifted peel corner), so the sticker attitude attaches to the hero widget; the glyph stays a solid ring plus numeral, and the peel becomes the launch/hover animation.

evaluations.verdict: A good illustration and a bad mark: three white-bordered objects plus confetti fight at 64px, turn to mush at 16px, lose the card and confetti to a circle mask, and the glyph (grey tab, star, half ring) never reads as one idea. It shows exactly what the board looks like, which is why it belongs in the empty state, not the Dock.
evaluations.riff: Demote it to the system's illustration layer: widen this exact scene for the empty board, onboarding and store/README hero, and let the icon be only its hero, the ring.

evaluations.verdict: The glyph is one of the most legible and meaningful in the set (card plus a three-strip burst reads as 'celebration' even at 1x), but the colour icon is lopsided: a small card shoved lower-left, a quarter of the plate empty, strips like candy sticks. The confetti burst is a one-shot finale, not a loop, so it gives the system no loader.
evaluations.riff: Merge with slot: take slot's centred, larger card and fire pop's three strips from behind its top edge. Keep pop's glyph unchanged; it's the best randomiser glyph in the round.

evaluations.verdict: The most extensible system here: cells map one-to-one from icon to glyph, it sets the drawing language for every per-widget toolbar icon, and the launch animation writes itself (ring sweeps, light cycles to green, reel spins, star slaps; an empty bento is the empty state). As the master mark, though, it's the least daring and still a grid glyph where the client asked for one to be replaced; it collapses to four blobs at true 16px, circle masks clip the corner cells, and the traffic light is vertical when the app's is horizontal.
evaluations.riff: Take it off the app mark and make it the secondary family: per-widget toolbar and docs icons drawn in this style, plus a launch animation where the four cells come alive in sequence, with the traffic light turned horizontal to match the app.

evaluations.verdict: The punchiest flat poster rendering here, and its thick ring and bold 5 would animate and scale more cleanly than ring's soft bezel. But it's ring with a detour: the glyph drops the numeral and becomes 'C plus heart' (Health, favourites), the magenta heart isn't the app's heart sticker (blue/teal in the reference), and the heart hangs far enough off-centre to be clipped by circle masks.
evaluations.riff: Fold its flat, thick-ring poster rendering into ring as the finishing style, and drop the heart, or at least keep it inside the plate and put the 5 back in the glyph.

general: Seven of nine concepts reuse the rainbow ring, and only those built around a single centred disc (ring, runner, sticker) survive two tests the sheets don't show: true 1x at 16-18px (the sheets render at 2x, which flatters board, gridplus and duo) and the circle masks ChromeOS and Android apply to a PWA icon, which matters for a web-first classroom tool. Nobody has shown the mark moving, yet the three strongest ideas are defined by motion the app already has (the arc depleting, the hamster lapping, the reel spinning), so the next round should storyboard loader, launch, time's-up and empty states, plus a live menu-bar and favicon countdown. Also missing: an idle vs live glyph spec, one numeral decision (5 and 6 are both in play, and a static digit can read as a badge), and an in-app lockup with the wordmark. Push for convergence: ring as the master mark, the runner as its animated leading cap and mascot layer, the reel as a secondary motion, and board/bento demoted to the illustration and per-widget icon family. Get daring from motion and character, not more collage.

evaluations.verdict: This has the lowest trademark risk in the set and the only glyph that still reads at 18px in all four bars. The problem is that an open arc around a bold 5 looks like Apple's skip-back-5 media symbol (gobackward.5) without its arrowhead, or a speed-limit sign in outline, and a 5 that never changes, sitting next to the clock, looks like live status ('5 minutes left?', '5 unread?'). The smooth rainbow ring is also the current look for AI features (Meta AI's gradient ring, Siri's glowing screen edge) and a well-worn Pomodoro-timer cliché, so as drawn it will look very 2025 by 2029.
evaluations.riff: Make the menu-bar item a live glyph: show the real minutes left inside an arc that shrinks while a timer runs. When idle, close the ring (draw the used-up part as a hairline instead of a gap) and put one dot on the rim where the runner sits. That single change removes the static-5, skip-back and loading-spinner readings.

evaluations.verdict: This is the only character in the set the brand could own, but as drawn the hamster isn't running on the ring, it's diving through the middle of it. That reads as 'jumping through hoops', and a hamster in a ring is the 'hamster wheel' idiom for pointless grind: two jokes teachers will make about a tool meant to lighten their workload. A cartoon hamster in a gold circle also recalls the Hamster Kombat crypto clicker game, and in the glyph the hamster turns into an ink blot at 18px.
evaluations.riff: Shrink the creature to a small runner on the rim at the leading end of the arc, as in the app, so the ring stays the hero. If a creature has to stay, use the bee: the fox reads as Firefox, the penguin as Linux's Tux (confusing in a GNOME bar), the tortoise says 'slow', and anything running in a ring says 'hamster wheel'.

evaluations.verdict: A purple-to-pink-to-amber gradient inside a white-framed rounded rectangle is Instagram's colour signature, and that 2016-era sunset gradient already looks dated. The chunky 3D yellow bar and faceted navy diamond read as a gold bar and a sapphire above a slot-reel window, which is jackpot/gacha imagery on a tool that picks children. The glyph (a wide rounded rectangle with a bar inside) sits next to the system battery icon and looks like one; with the two flecks above it becomes a face or a toaster.
evaluations.riff: Turn the card and the glyph upright: a vertical reel with the chosen chip solid and the neighbouring chips cut off above and below, plus a bold initial in the chosen chip. Flatten the confetti into plain paper strips so nothing reads as gems, gold or a battery.

evaluations.verdict: This is the most literal answer to 'the rainbow timer and the name picker', but a round lettered badge at bottom-left overlapping a coloured card at top-right is how Microsoft's Office and Teams icons are built. Next to Word and Teams in a Windows taskbar, it reads as another Microsoft 365 app. The glyph (a C-ring hooked onto a slotted square) reads as a chain-link 'copy link' icon or a coin going into a slot, the 5 disappears at 16px, and the corner card falls outside the safe circle of a masked PWA icon.
evaluations.riff: Reduce it to one round shape: tuck the name card behind the dial as a small tab peeking out at its upper-right rim, like a name tag clipped to the timer. In the glyph, draw that tab as a single notch on the ring rather than a second object.

evaluations.verdict: This is the warmest colour icon in the set, the star alone carries it at 16px, and a gold star means praise in any classroom. But the monochrome glyph, a grey C opening to the right with a five-pointed star in its mouth, is almost exactly ☪: the star and crescent of the Turkish and Malaysian flags, and close to Singapore's. For a Singapore company selling into Malaysia, Indonesia and the Gulf, that's a showstopper until the glyph is redrawn. The arc is also drawn in half-opacity grey, so it nearly disappears in the dark Windows and GNOME bars.
evaluations.riff: Redraw the glyph with the ring closed behind the star (the used-up part as a thinner stroke, with only a hairline gap around the star). Move the star up onto the rim at 1–2 o'clock, where the runner sits, so the shape reads as 'a star badge on a dial' and never as 'a star in a crescent's mouth'.

evaluations.verdict: This is a screenshot, not a mark: three objects plus confetti turn to mush below 32px. The glyph (a lumpy grey card, a star and an open C) reads as the 'clear night, partly cloudy' weather icon (cloud, moon, star) that the Windows taskbar already shows, with a star-beside-a-crescent echo on top. It is also the concept most tied to the current widget designs, so it dates the moment any widget is restyled.
evaluations.riff: Drop it as the icon and use it as marketing or About-screen artwork. Carry only its idea of a sticker slapped over the join into the single-dial direction.

evaluations.verdict: Confetti bursting off a card is the stock 'success' illustration from countless onboarding screens, and here the card is small in a mostly empty tile. The tray glyph (a wide rounded rectangle with burst lines at one corner) reads as a battery throwing sparks, meaning either charging or an electrical fault. The card also carries the same Instagram-gradient association as slot, and the top-right confetti is the first thing a circular PWA icon mask cuts off.
evaluations.riff: Fold it into slot: one large, centred, upright reel card as the only hero, with at most two flat paper-strip flecks inside the safe circle, and no burst lines in the glyph.

evaluations.verdict: The client asked to get rid of the grid, and this is the grid again. Four mini-widgets on a tile is the standard icon for dashboard and home-screen-widget apps. A white 2×2 cluster in the Windows tray reads as the Start or Widgets button, and at 16px four coloured quadrants recall the Microsoft logo. The promised bento compartments aren't actually drawn, bento layouts are a 2023–25 trend that will date, and the glossy navy traffic light is the coldest, heaviest element in an otherwise warm set.
evaluations.riff: Replace the 2×2 with the rainbow dial alone at full size, which is effectively the ring concept. Nothing about the grid framing survives the client's brief.

evaluations.verdict: This is the boldest and least trend-dependent drawing in the set (a flat dial filling the tile), and it holds up at 16px. But a rainbow ring plus a pink heart is the classic Pride motif: welcome in many schools, but a procurement flag where rainbow imagery is regulated (Malaysia seized rainbow Swatch watches in 2023), and the heart also pulls it toward health, dating and 'like' apps. The glyph, a thick C with a heart at its open end, reads as a refresh arrow or the letter G.
evaluations.riff: Swap the heart for the die-cut gold star (praise rather than love, which also removes the rainbow-and-heart reading). Put it on the rim at 1–2 o'clock over a closed ring in the glyph, and use this flat dial as the base for merging ring and sticker.

general: Seven of nine concepts rely on the smooth rainbow ring, and that one element carries most of the set's risk. It is the current visual shorthand for AI features (Meta AI's gradient ring, Siri's glowing screen edge), it reads as a Pride motif in markets that regulate rainbow imagery (most strongly when paired with a heart), and at 16px it blends into the four-colour Google Workspace icons that fill every teacher's browser tabs, so the next round should test a rainbow dial split into segments with tick marks and a numeral, which keeps the recognition but loses the glowing-halo look. Every concept also sits on the same low-poly amber tile, a 2014-era texture that vanishes below 64px and clashes with macOS 26's tinted and clear icon modes, and the multi-object compositions (board, gridplus, duo, pop, slot) will turn to mush in tinted mode and lose corner elements to circular PWA and Android icon masks. Most glyphs are shrunken illustrations that look like system icons: a battery (slot, pop), a refresh arrow or letter G (dial2), skip-back-5 or a notification count (ring), night-time weather (board), ☪ (sticker) and a chain link (duo), so the glyph should be drawn as a sign first, with a closed outline, and could show the live timer. Round 3 should converge on one flat dial with a single die-cut gold star on its rim (merging ring, dial2 and sticker), keep any numeral to 5 or 6 (never 4, which sounds like 'death' in Chinese, Japanese and Korean), and run a trademark search plus browser-tab, tinted-mode and 16px tray tests before anything ships.
